DSL.TITLE: Document Ranking in a Mobile World
DSL.COMMENT: As higher education becomes more competitive, administrators look to IT solutions to get the edge over other higher education institutions to raise enrollment.  Due to the performance funding model and budgetary decreases in education, the edge has become more important than it ever has.  As technology progresses, many studies show that more and more searches are being completed via mobile devices.   When looking at student behavior, document ranking among browsers is mainly done by a linear approach, such as single-domain-related ranking that ranks based on a specific vertical vector.  The core component of the vertical search is relevance ranking, which is how search engines rank individual websites in terms of importance or weight.  For example, Google’s PageRank, uses their patented algorithm to place a numerical value to every web page in its search index based largely on popularity and the number of sites that are connected to the site.  The algorithm also accounts the popularity of the other sites that are linked to the main site, which will increase the numerical value depending on how popular the child sites are.  In many cases, just because a site is the most popular does not mean it is the most relevant.  While PageRank provides the ranking for individual pages, Google uses TrustFlow to rank a collection of sites.  Between these two systems, Google provides the ranking to its customers as they search for pages; however, there is a tradeoff between the overall relevance between a query and a document or website.  To solve this problem, search engines that are content based or that have a specific domain can dramatically improve the quality and value to the user.  To prove this point even further,  J. Yu from Search Engine Land stated that recent research that mobile “accounts for as much as 57 percent of the total search traffic”.  As search engines develop, this percentage will increase.  Vertical search engines are divided into categories and provide analysis for one specific kind of content.  As more and more vertical search engines come online, the potential for more fragmentation will occur unless searches are more personalized and mobile friendly.  Here is the share of web searches via Jumpshot; however, this does not account for how much is mobile.

DSL.TITLE: Valleyfragrances.com
DSL.COMMENT: The initial idea of the project was to make a basic website that would display all readily available stock for the Gold Palace shop located in McAllen, TX. After several iterations of the project, the team came to the decision to add several other functions to the website. This is because the owner of Gold Palace is looking to have a payment option to order online and have perfume products shipped.  This document will go through the design and implementation of a website and database that allows for an e-commerce store to function. The website must be able to store and manage perfume, customer, and purchase information in the database. The website must be able to present various forms of information to the customer and the admin depending on what is needed. There must be an integration of the Paypal API to allow the customer to make a purchase and have that purchase stored. This requires a database that has many kinds of tables storing information related to each other and done so in a way that all data can be accessed as needed.

DSL.COMMENT: Not all math problems we solve are a straight equation to solve for. SCHTEACH.PEDINN:
CSCI/CMPE 3333 teaches you algorithms, data structures, and software principles -- those being fundamentals needed as essential groundwork for making the rest journey of learning computer science. It emphasizes fundamental questions of computer science: how to organize large amount of data and how to design algorithms to process large amount data efficiently in time and space. It covers the following topics: 
•	Algorithms design and analysis: greedy algorithms, divide and conquer, dynamic programming, randomize algorithms, backtracking algorithms, graph algorithms, and amortized analysis, computational complexity, P vs. NP problems. 
•	Data structures: lists, stacks, queues, sets, trees, and graphs. 
•	Hashing: hashing functions, separate chaining, open addressing, rehashing, and extendible hashing. 
•	Sorting: various methods including heapsort, mergesort, quicksort, indirect sorting, bucket sorting, and external sorting.
SCHTEACH.TECHMAT: There six programming projects and 11 lab exercises.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Developing Randomization and Alberization for Algorithms and Complexity Theory
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Computational theory serves as the backbone of Computer Science, providing a large number of fundamental
mathematical tools which underpin Computer Science’s many sub-fields. However, as its tool set has
matured and expanded, so has the influence of computational theory. This synergistic combination serves to
make it even more important to continue the pursuit of fundamental advances in computational theory and
the tools it provides to its ever broadening sphere of influence. In this proposal, the PIs demonstrate a plan
for making great strides in further developing two such newly emerging and important tools, randomization
and algebrization.

While randomness has long been viewed as a nuisance in mathematics and something to be avoided or
minimized, extremely powerful methods of harnessing its power for the design of randomized algorithms have
recently cast it in a whole new light. Randomization has allowed for the creation of extremely powerful and
efficient algorithms that were otherwise unobtainable. Another tool, algebrization, provides methods for the
reformulation of a diversity of problems into forms in which the highly developed tools of algebra can be
brought to bear on them. These two sets of tools provide a powerful platform from which to attack a broad
and important set of crucial open problems on the boundaries of computational complexity and algorithmic
development, and the PIs form a group of scientists uniquely qualified to attack and solve these problems.

One target is the further development of the theory of testing monomials in multivariate polynomials.
The complexity portion of research in this area was initiated by the PIs, and the resultant theory has found
applications in areas such as graph algorithms, Bioinformatics, and wireless networking. The complexity
aspects of the monomial testing problem and its variants will be extensively investigated with two objectives.
One is to understand how this problem may be related to critical problems in complexity, and if so to what
extent. The other is to exploit possibilities of applying algebraic properties of polynomials to the study of
those problems. Of particular interests are separations among fundamental complexity classes. Secondly,
the PIs plan to use randomized and algebraic methods to tackle a set of problems in the field of exact and
parameterized tractable computation, an active and developing field in recent years. By applying randomized
and algebraic techniques, the PIs will develop faster exact and parameterized algorithms for, and study lower
bounds of, a set of well-known graph problems (e.g. the Hamiltonian cycle problem). Another direction of
the work consists of studying problems in the field of computational learning theory which are closely related,
and amenable, to the techniques of randomization and algebrization.

The two PIs work in the same department, have very strong research records in each of the areas listed
above, have great familiarity with the tools of randomization and algebrization, have worked closely together
on a large set of successful collaborations, and continually maintain close ties through research projects and
seminars. This combination puts them in a position to make important advances across the wide range of
the projects proposed.

Intellectual merit of the proposed activities: Randomization is a basic tool of algorithm design applicable
to many problems. Algebrization has significant importance in both algorithm design and computational
complexity theory. As this proposal combines algebrization with randomization, the results of the proposed
research will make new contributions to the core area of computational theory and discover new applications
in the fields of Bioinformatics and computational learning theory. It is anticipated that new algebraic and
derandomization techniques will be developed for testing monomials and the results thereof may lead to
possible breakthroughs in areas of complexity class separation and parameterized computation.

Broader impacts of the proposed activities: The University of Texas-Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV),
located in the South Texas Rio Grande Valley area, has more than 28,000 students. UTRGV is the largest
university in the US to have a majority Hispanic student population: 90% of its students are Hispanics,
including 59% females. An important part of this proposal is to support underrepresented minority and
female graduate and undergraduate students. We plan to develop a randomized computation course and
propose a set of applied algorithm projects for both undergraduate and graduate students at UTRGV. These
will attract participation of female and male engineers/scientists from the Hispanic community to pursue
research in Computer Science. The training and experiences obtained by those students through the proposed
research endeavors will lay a stepping-stone for them to land at fruitful careers in areas of science, technology,
engineering and mathematics.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: In this paper, we develop an exponential time approximation scheme for the traveling salesman problem (TSP) on undirected graphs.
